title: So you had a near-death experience. Now what?
excerpt: In new UChicago Divinity course, students read accounts of the briefly deceased through the lens of anthropology and Islamic thought
content:
Editor’s Note: This is part of a series called UChicago Class Visits, spotlighting transformative classroom experiences and unique learning opportunities offered at UChicago.

As Elham Mireshghi walked around the International Association for Near-Death Studies conference, her anthropologist antenna was buzzing.

People previously on the brink of death had returned from the veil with wondrous visions. As they compared their experiences, patterns emerged: tunnels of light, visits from deceased loved ones, encounters with divine beings. 

Many believed they’d seen God. 

“I was constantly thinking that there is a very interesting social-political dimension to all of this,” said Mireshghi, an associate instructional professor at the University of Chicago Divinity School. Here is this community being built around these spiritual experiences.”

The community around near-death experiences, also known as NDEs, seemed to be borrowing from many different religious traditions to help interpret their meanings—with a major exception.

“I was the only visibly Muslim person there,” Mireshghi said.

In Witnessing the Afterlife: Anthropological and Islamic Approaches to Near-Death Experiences, a new course offered by the University of Chicago Divinity School, students grapple with these accounts in an academic setting. Each week, a mix of graduate and College students, with interests ranging from end-of-life care to the paranormal, read religious texts alongside first-hand testimonials.

“The class and the questions that we're asking are an attempt to bring a largely overlooked swath of human experience—a record of human consciousness—into dialogue,” said Yousef Casewit, an associate professor of Qur'anic Studies who co-teaches the course with Mireshghi.

In the following edited Q&A, Mireshghi and Casewit discuss how near-death experiences are culturally influenced, how they align with or challenge existing theology, and what Islamic thought can bring to their interpretation. 

How does this course fit into your own scholarship?

Casewit: As a scholar of medieval Islamic thought, I often return to questions of the imagination. 

Many medieval thinkers, such as Ibn ‘Arabi (d. 1240), described an imaginal realm as an intermediary world between the physical world we observe through our senses and a transcendent world beyond them. There, abstract ideas take on concrete forms, as in visions, mystical experiences, dreams, UFO abductions, encounters with Jinn, and, I'd argue, NDEs.

Mireshghi: I have been personally curious about NDEs for some time, but they also fit within my research on brain death and organ transplantation, which raises interesting questions about human consciousness, the body and death. 

Given my research focus on Iran, I see important parallels between the recent popularization of NDEs as Islamically legitimated encounters with the otherworldly and Iran’s distinctive efforts to promote organ transplantation within an Islamic framework.

What is a near-death experience or NDE?

Mireshghi: Within scientific discourse, NDEs are often associated with clinical death, marked by the cessation of heartbeat and breathing. However, researchers such as Bruce Greyson also include similar experiences occurring under conditions of extreme danger, for example, moments before a car accident. 

As an anthropologist, I'm less interested in specific definitions than in understanding how those definitions come into being.

What makes NDEs appear to be a new phenomenon, I think, is that they are increasingly reported in hospital settings, often corroborated by doctors or other medical professionals. This lends them a degree of scientific legitimacy that distinguishes them from earlier accounts of otherworldly encounters.

What are some common things people see during a near-death experience?

Casewit: Experiencers often describe these episodes as more real than ordinary waking life. Many involve a visceral, lucid meeting with people who shaped them. They can raise questions like: Were you loved in your life? Are you at peace with who you are?

Mireshghi: A tunnel of light, being guided by a spiritual entity, telepathic communication with such entities, foreshadowing of future events, and a feeling of being “at home,” as though returning to the womb, are commonly reported. 

Many also experience a “life review,” where they not only witness their lives replayed but undergo a shift in subjectivity, experiencing the effects of their actions from the perspectives of other humans, animals and even plants. 

What are some differences between reports of near-death experiences in the Western world and the Islamic one?

Casewit: What's in the water where you grow up shapes how the experience is structured, and how it's told.

In North America, NDEs tend to be expressed in a particular idiom. American NDEers often report encounters with Jesus or angelic figures from the Christian biblical tradition.

Christianity has a long visionary tradition, but many congregations today offer little vocabulary for these experiences. So, some NDEers turn to a more open-ended, pluralistic, sometimes perennialist view that all religions share a common core, centered on love and interconnectedness of all things.

Accounts from Muslim backgrounds more often foreground questions of accountability: What did you do? How can you make right the wrongs you committed? The Qur’an stresses the importance of being aware of one’s mortality—that death can come at any moment—and this awareness is understood as a call to ethical change.

How do NDEs challenge or fold into existing worldviews—either religious or scientific?

Casewit: NDEs can unsettle two very different frameworks: a materialist, scientistic worldview that reduces consciousness to brain activity, and exclusivist theologies that see salvation as belonging to one tradition alone.

Neither leaves much room for the imaginal realm, so NDEs can be hard to make sense of. Skeptical scientists and religious gatekeepers alike tend to dismiss them as mere anecdotes.

Mireshghi: In secular Western contexts, some people who have NDEs end up becoming estranged from their family members. We see reports of depression and divorce, in part because their communities lack shared religious idioms that can make sense of these extraordinary, typically transformative experiences. 

Even in Muslim contexts, people may shy away from sharing their NDEs, because such numinous encounters are often associated with spiritual adepts rather than ordinary people. Yet, Islamic theology and eschatology, particularly interpretations touched by the Ishraqi tradition, offer rich metaphysical frameworks for making sense of NDEs. We’re now seeing growing interest in interpreting them from the Islamic perspective. 

I would say the greatest challenge to Islamic theology is what some experiencers describe as “past lives.”

What do you hope students take away from the course?

Mireshghi: As an anthropologist, I hope to equip students with conceptual tools to ask interesting questions on their own. 

At the same time, there’s a glaring gap in the Western discourse on NDEs when it comes to the experiences of Muslims and the conceptual and theological resources that Islam may offer. We hope the course begins to address that.

Casewit: Near-death experiences go to the heart of what it means to be human. Making sense of them requires radical interdisciplinarity: disciplines with very different tools working together to develop nuanced ways of speaking about consciousness and the nature of reality. 

The more perspectives, the merrier.
